newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech coalition launches new economic package.
newsitem.headline: Czech coalition launches new economic package.

text.p: The three parties in the ruling Czech coalition agreed on Wednesday to a series of emergency steps to help revive a sagging economy.
These included budget cuts, public sector wage freezes and ministerial changes.
Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said the country must expect economic decline and a significant rise in unemployment, but that the plan was aimed at restoring growth as quickly as possible.
The new package of measures agreed by the coalition and announced by Klaus at a news conference include:
* a freeze in the total volume of public sector wages and budget cuts leading to a balanced budget in 1997
* a "slightly" surplus budget in 1998
* support for the restrictive monetary policies of the central bank to minimalise inflation and the reduce current account deficit
* restrictions on imports financed from the public sector budget
* negotiations with unions on stemming wage growth
* support for foreign exchange measures of the central bank to strengthen the stability of the crown
Last week the coalition leaders agreed to make changes in the cabinet amid a sharp drop in approval ratings, an economic downturn, and an attack by speculators on the Czech crown.
Klaus said Education Minister Ivan Pilip would take over in the key post of finance minister and current Czech ambassador to Britain Karel Kuhnl would be the new Industry and Trade Minister.
Pavel Necas would be the new Interior Minister and Jiri Grusa would take the education portfolio.

Klaus said that if the measures did not lead to an improvement in the foreign currency and trade situation by the second half of the year, the coalition would consider further import restrictions including possibly higher tariffs, import surcharges, or "non-tariff measures."
"Instead of growth of the economy we have to expect rather a decline accompanied by a significant increase in unemployment," Klaus said.
The coalition also called on the central bank to take measures to strengthen the stability of the crown, but no specific measures were specified.

The Czech crown has come under heavy attack and the central bank on Monday was forced to abandon its fluctation band and the currency float. Since the Monday announcement, the crown dropped by roughly seven percent against the dollar and mark, although it firmed slightly on Wednesday.
Analysts have forecast already that the Czech economy could slow to near zero growth in 1997 after 4.4 percent real growth in 1996.
Unemployment in April stood at 3.8 percent, but many economists have said the figure is artificially low because of a lack of restructuring in Czech industry.
"Low unemployment in this situation is rather a result of... unfavourable phenomena than an expression of a dynamically developing economy," the coalition agreement said.
The economy has been hampered by a bulging current account deficit which equals about nine percent of gross domestic product, and lagging productivity.
The announced plans on Wednesday are to be added on top of an austerity programme already announced in April which made more than 20 billion crowns in budget cuts, Klaus said.

The ministerial changes filled positions vacated last weekend by Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik, Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy, and Interior Minister Jan Ruml who resigned at meetings of their party leaderships.
-- John Mastrini, Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
